name: Yukawa potential as a screened Coulomb Green's function
summary: Yukawa built the nuclear force by giving the electrostatic field a mass. The static potential is the Green's function of the screened Poisson equation and reduces to Coulomb's law as μ→0; its range ħ/m_πc ≈ 1.4 fm predicted the pion. One-pion exchange is still the long-range part of every modern chiral-EFT potential.
breaks: The pion is a pseudoscalar isovector, so one-pion exchange has spin–isospin and tensor structure that Coulomb's law lacks. The short-range core, two-pion exchange and three-nucleon forces have no electrostatic analogue.
sources: Yukawa (1935). "On the Interaction of Elementary Particles. I". *Proc. Phys.-Math. Soc. Jpn.* 17, 48. [doi:10.11429/ppmsj1919.17.0_48](https://doi.org/10.11429/ppmsj1919.17.0_48)

name: Fermi density effect in ionization energy loss
summary: At high βγ the polarization of the medium screens distant collisions and reduces the relativistic rise of the Bethe stopping power by the density-effect term δ. δ depends on the medium's dielectric response through its plasma frequency. Fermi's 1940 dielectric treatment showed that the same polarization field radiates Cherenkov light wherever ε(ω) > 1/β^2.

name: Debye screening of colour and quarkonium melting
summary: Free colour charges screen the static quark–antiquark potential the same way mobile charges screen a Coulomb field, with dielectric function ε(k) = 1 + m_D^2/k^2. Heavy quarkonia therefore dissolve once the Debye length becomes smaller than their size. Matsui and Satz proposed J/ψ suppression as a QGP signature on this basis.
breaks: Colour is non-Abelian and magnetic screening is non-perturbative. The imaginary part of the in-medium potential (Landau damping) dominates dissociation, and at the LHC charm quarks recombine to regenerate J/ψ.
sources: Matsui & Satz (1986). "J/ψ suppression by quark-gluon plasma formation". *Phys. Lett. B* 178, 416. [doi:10.1016/0370-2693(86)91404-8](https://doi.org/10.1016/0370-2693(86)91404-8)

name: MAC-E filter: adiabatic magnetic collimation in KATRIN
summary: KATRIN's MAC-E filter uses a slowly varying magnetic field, so the adiabatic invariant p_⊥^2/B turns almost all transverse momentum of tritium β electrons into longitudinal motion against an electrostatic retarding potential. This gives an energy resolution ΔE/E = B_min/B_max and sub-eV limits on the neutrino mass.

name: Flow eccentricities as multipole moments of the fireball
summary: The initial shape of the fireball is decomposed into azimuthal multipole moments of its entropy density, the eccentricities ε_n, and hydrodynamics turns them almost linearly into flow harmonics v_n. A deformed nucleus adds its quadrupole (β_2) to ε_2, so flow data now image the deformation of 238U and 129Xe. This links back to nuclear quadrupole moments.
map: \varepsilon_ne^{in\Phi_n}=-\frac{\int r^ne^{in\phi}s(\mathbf r)\,d^2r}{\int r^ns(\mathbf r)\,d^2r},\ \ v_n\approx\kappa_n\varepsilon_n,\ \ \langle\varepsilon_2^2\rangle\approx a+b\beta_2^2
breaks: These are 2D cylindrical moments of an entropy density, not 3D spherical moments of a charge. The response is viscous and partly non-linear rather than a static field.

name: Nuclear multipole moments and deformation
summary: Nuclear charge and current distributions are described by the same spherical multipoles as in electrostatics. Magnetic dipole and electric quadrupole moments test the shell model (Schmidt lines, single-particle Q), and the intrinsic quadrupole of a deformed nucleus is the l=2 multipole of its surface. Both are measured through the quadrupole–field-gradient coupling in atomic hyperfine structure and through Coulomb-excitation B(E2) values.

name: Laser isotope separation
summary: When isotope shifts exceed the Doppler width, narrow-band lasers can selectively ionize or dissociate one isotope (AVLIS on atomic vapour, molecular schemes on UF6). The technique is used for uranium enrichment, for laser-ionized radioactive beams, and increasingly for medical-isotope precursors.

name: Muonic-hydrogen laser spectroscopy of the proton radius
summary: Pulsed laser spectroscopy of the 2S–2P Lamb shift in muonic hydrogen, at about 6 μm, gave a proton charge radius of 0.84 fm, ten times more precise than before; it started the proton-radius puzzle. Frequency-comb spectroscopy of ordinary hydrogen and new electron-scattering data now largely agree with it.
sources: Pohl et al. (2010). "The size of the proton". *Nature* 466, 213. [doi:10.1038/nature09250](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature09250)

name: Laser-driven inertial fusion of D–T
summary: Inertial confinement fusion uses lasers as the driver. NIF's 192 frequency-tripled (351 nm) Nd:glass beams heat a hohlraum whose X-rays implode a D–T capsule, and since December 2022 some shots have released more fusion energy than the laser energy delivered to the target. Nonlinear-optical frequency conversion, beam smoothing and laser–plasma instabilities set the performance limits.

name: Laser spectroscopy of radii and moments of rare isotopes
summary: Collinear and resonance-ionization laser spectroscopy measure the spins, magnetic and quadrupole moments and charge radii of short-lived isotopes from hyperfine structure and isotope shifts. The results reveal shell closures, halos and unexpected radius trends such as the large radii of neutron-rich calcium, and the method has reached nobelium. Resonance laser ion sources also provide element-selective radioactive beams.

name: Giant dipole resonance as a nuclear plasmon
summary: The giant dipole resonance, in which protons oscillate against neutrons, is a nuclear analogue of the localized surface plasmon of a metal nanoparticle. Both are a single Lorentzian collective dipole mode that exhausts the dipole sum rule (Thomas–Reiche–Kuhn in nuclei, the f-sum rule in optics). Metal-cluster physicists describe the cluster's Mie plasmon in the same language.
breaks: The restoring force is the nuclear symmetry energy, not Coulomb attraction, and both fluids move. The GDR energy falls with size (~A^-1/3), whereas the quasi-static plasmon frequency ω_p/√3 does not depend on size.

name: Light-by-light scattering in ultraperipheral collisions
summary: The QED vacuum's Euler–Heisenberg four-photon coupling is the vacuum analogue of an optical χ^(3) Kerr nonlinearity. It was first seen as light-by-light scattering γγ → γγ in ultra-peripheral Pb–Pb collisions, using the quasi-real photon clouds of the nuclei (ATLAS evidence 2017, later CMS and ATLAS observations). The related Breit–Wheeler process γγ → e+e− is also measured there.
map: \mathcal L_{\rm EH}=\frac{2\alpha^2}{45m_e^4}\big[(\mathbf E^2-\mathbf B^2)^2+7(\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf B)^2\big]\ \ (\text{natural units})
breaks: The Euler–Heisenberg Lagrangian is only the low-energy limit ω ≪ m_e, and UPC photon pairs at GeV energies probe the full box diagram. Laser vacuum-birefringence searches such as PVLAS have not yet reached the effective-Lagrangian signal.

name: VUV frequency comb for the Th-229 nuclear clock
summary: The 8.36 eV isomer of 229Th was excited with VUV lasers in 2024 and resolved with a VUV frequency comb made by cavity-enhanced seventh-harmonic generation of an infrared comb. The comb measured the transition's frequency ratio to the 87Sr optical clock and resolved its nuclear electric-quadrupole splitting in a CaF2 host. This makes a nuclear transition a candidate optical clock with enhanced sensitivity to variations of fundamental constants.

name: Cherenkov and transition-radiation detectors
summary: Cherenkov emission (cosθ_C = 1/nβ, Frank–Tamm photon yield) and transition radiation (yield ∝ γ) are the basis of threshold counters, ring-imaging Cherenkov detectors and TRDs. These identify electrons, pions and other hadrons in nuclear-physics spectrometers and the EIC's ePIC detector, and water-Cherenkov detectors use the same light to detect neutrinos. The Cherenkov angle gives β, which together with momentum gives the particle's mass.

name: Gamma-decay multipolarity is multipole radiation
summary: Nuclear γ transitions are classified as electric and magnetic 2^L-pole radiation and follow the selection rules of classical multipole radiation (EL parity (-1)^L, ML parity (-1)^(L+1)). Weisskopf single-particle estimates are the antenna formulas with nuclear transition moments inserted, and each extra multipole order costs a factor of about (kR)^2 ~ 10^-3–10^-5. That suppression is why high-L or very low-energy transitions give long-lived isomers such as the 8.4 eV M1 isomer of 229Th.

name: Bremsstrahlung, radiation length and showers
summary: Above the critical energy, electrons lose energy mainly by bremsstrahlung in nuclear Coulomb fields, the relativistic radiation of a decelerated charge. The radiation length X0 then sets how electromagnetic showers develop in calorimeters. Because the radiative-to-collisional loss ratio grows roughly as EZ, β shielding puts low-Z material first.

name: Synchrotron radiation and Sokolov–Ternov polarization
summary: Synchrotron power scales as γ^4/ρ^2; it limits the energy of electron storage rings and sets the EIC electron ring at up to 18 GeV. Spin-flip synchrotron emission self-polarizes stored electrons antiparallel to the field (Sokolov–Ternov, 92.4%), which HERA exploited. The EIC needs both helicities and self-polarization is slow, so it instead refreshes bunches from a polarized source while fighting radiative depolarization.
sources: Schwinger (1949). "On the Classical Radiation of Accelerated Electrons". *Phys. Rev.* 75, 1912. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.75.1912](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.75.1912)

name: LPM suppression and QCD radiative energy loss
summary: When the formation time of a radiated quantum exceeds the mean free path, successive scatterings act coherently and suppress the radiation; for bremsstrahlung in dense matter this is the Landau–Pomeranchuk–Migdal effect. The BDMPS-Z and GLV radiative energy loss of quarks and gluons in the QGP is its non-Abelian version, governed by the transport coefficient q̂.
breaks: The radiated gluon carries colour and rescatters itself, which gives ΔE ∝ q̂L^2 rather than the QED scaling. The medium is also a rapidly expanding, strongly coupled plasma rather than a static solid.

name: Cyclotron radiation spectroscopy of tritium β electrons
summary: Project 8 measures β-electron energies from the frequency of their cyclotron radiation, f_c = eB/2πγm_e (~26 GHz near 1 T), picked up in a waveguide; the signal power is the Larmor power of a circulating charge. The goal is the neutrino mass from the tritium endpoint, and the experiment has already set a first tritium limit.

name: Laser Compton backscattering gamma sources
summary: Backscattering laser or FEL photons off relativistic electrons (inverse Compton scattering) produces tunable, quasi-monoenergetic, highly polarized MeV γ beams, as at HIγS. These beams are used to measure photonuclear cross sections and giant resonances, and for nuclear resonance fluorescence assays that identify specific isotopes.

name: Photon attenuation: photoelectric, Compton, pair
summary: Gamma-ray detection and shielding rest on the photon–matter cross sections of light-scattering theory: photoabsorption, Compton scattering with the Klein–Nishina cross section (which reduces to Thomson's σ_T at low energy), and pair production. Together these set the exponential attenuation coefficient μ(E,Z). The Compton edge and continuum seen in every γ spectrum follow directly from Compton kinematics.

name: Compton scattering off the nucleon: Thomson to DVCS
summary: Real Compton scattering off the nucleon has the low-energy structure of light scattering: a Thomson amplitude fixed by charge and mass, then a Rayleigh-like ω^2 term set by the electric and magnetic polarizabilities. The values α_E ≈ 11×10^-4 fm^3 and β_M ≈ 2.5×10^-4 fm^3 show the proton is a very stiff object. Deeply virtual Compton scattering is the same process in the Bjorken limit, where it accesses GPDs and the Ji spin sum rule.

name: Compton profiles and Bjorken scaling
summary: X-ray Compton profiles and Bjorken scaling in deep inelastic scattering are both impulse-approximation results. At large momentum transfer the probe scatters off quasi-free constituents, so the cross section depends on a single scaling variable and measures their momentum distribution: J(p_z) for electrons, q(x) for quarks. y-scaling in quasi-elastic electron–nucleus scattering is the intermediate case, for nucleons.
breaks: Partons are confined and relativistic, so the scaling variable is a light-cone momentum fraction and the final state hadronizes instead of escaping. QCD radiation also produces logarithmic scaling violations (DGLAP), which atomic Compton profiles do not have.
sources: Bjorken (1969). "Asymptotic Sum Rules at Infinite Momentum". *Phys. Rev.* 179, 1547. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.179.1547](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.179.1547)

name: Optical model as nuclear Mie scattering
summary: Elastic nucleon–nucleus scattering is described by a complex potential whose imaginary part absorbs flux into other channels. This is the quantum counterpart of Mie scattering by a sphere with a complex refractive index: both use partial-wave series, separate elastic from absorption cross sections and obey the optical theorem. The name 'optical model' (the 'cloudy crystal ball') comes directly from this analogy.
map: \nabla^2\psi+k^2n^2\psi=0\ \leftrightarrow\ n^2(\mathbf r)=1-\frac{U(\mathbf r)}{E},\ U=-(V+iW)f(r);\ \ \sigma_{\rm tot}=\frac{4\pi}{k}{\rm Im}f(0)
breaks: Mie theory is vectorial, with two coefficient series a_n and b_n for polarization, and uses a local, energy-independent index. The nuclear potential is scalar plus spin–orbit, energy-dependent and nonlocal, and the long-range Coulomb field distorts the partial waves of charged projectiles.
sources: Mie (1908). "Beiträge zur Optik trüber Medien, speziell kolloidaler Metallösungen". *Ann. Phys.* 330, 377. [doi:10.1002/andp.19083300302](https://doi.org/10.1002/andp.19083300302)

name: Coherent backscattering, speckle and weak localization
summary: Time-reversed paths in a disordered medium interfere constructively. For light this gives the coherent-backscattering cone; for electrons it gives the weak-localization correction to the resistance. Universal conductance fluctuations are electronic speckle, a sample-specific fingerprint. Hanbury Brown–Twiss correlations reappear as electron antibunching and shot noise.
breaks: Light has no Fermi statistics, and for it absorption and moving scatterers play the role of dephasing. 3D Anderson localization of light has not been convincingly shown, and claims for TiO2 powders are contested.

name: The phase problem: crystallography and phase retrieval
summary: A far-field diffraction pattern is the squared Fourier transform of the scattering density, so the phase is lost. Crystallography's Patterson and direct methods and optics' iterative phase retrieval (Gerchberg–Saxton, Fienup) attack the same problem. Combined with oversampling they gave coherent diffractive imaging at synchrotrons and XFELs, and Gabor invented holography for electron microscopy.
map: I(\mathbf q)=|\tilde\rho(\mathbf q)|^2\Leftrightarrow P(\mathbf r)=\int\rho(\mathbf r')\rho(\mathbf r'+\mathbf r)\,d^3r'

name: Electron optics: Snell's law and Veselago lens at p–n junctions
summary: Ballistic Dirac electrons crossing a graphene p–n junction refract according to Snell's law with an effective index ∝ ±k_F. On the hole side the index is negative, so a p–n junction acts as a Veselago lens (Cheianov–Fal'ko–Altshuler). Klein tunnelling sets the angle-dependent transmission, and focusing has been seen in hBN-encapsulated devices.
breaks: λ_F is comparable to device features, so ray optics is only approximate. Smooth junctions collimate electrons toward normal incidence instead of imaging. Pseudospin conservation (Klein tunnelling) has no optical counterpart, and disorder and electron–electron scattering limit coherence.
sources: Castro Neto et al. (2009). "The electronic properties of graphene". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 81, 109. [arXiv:0709.1163](https://arxiv.org/abs/0709.1163)

name: SQUID double slit and Josephson Fraunhofer pattern
summary: A DC SQUID is a two-slit interferometer for the condensate, and the critical current of one wide junction in a field follows the single-slit Fraunhofer pattern. In general I_c(Φ) is the modulus of the Fourier transform of the critical-current density J_c(x), and Fourier-optics inversion (Dynes–Fulton) uses this to image supercurrent paths.
breaks: The phase belongs to a macroscopic condensate, not to a light field, and the junction dynamics are nonlinear. The pattern is distorted by self-screening (β_L≳1) and by a Josephson length λ_J shorter than the junction. The measured quantity is a critical current, not an intensity.
sources: Josephson (1962). "Possible new effects in superconductive tunnelling". *Phys. Lett.* 1, 251. [doi:10.1016/0031-9163(62)91369-0](https://doi.org/10.1016/0031-9163(62)91369-0)

name: Electron quantum optics with quantum Hall edge channels
summary: Chiral quantum Hall edge channels serve as lossless one-way beam paths and quantum point contacts as tunable beam splitters. Together they build electronic Mach–Zehnder and Fabry–Pérot interferometers, which show Aharonov–Bohm oscillations and electronic Hanbury Brown–Twiss and Hong–Ou–Mandel effects. Fabry–Pérot interferometry has also measured the braiding phase of ν=1/3 anyons.
breaks: Electrons are fermions, so they antibunch and obey Pauli exclusion. Coulomb charging effects dominate small Fabry–Pérot devices, and interactions between edge channels cause dephasing and energy relaxation, which limit visibility in a way photons do not.

name: Neumann's principle: crystal system fixes optical class
summary: The dielectric tensor must be invariant under the crystal's point group. Cubic crystals are optically isotropic; tetragonal, trigonal and hexagonal ones are uniaxial; orthorhombic, monoclinic and triclinic ones are biaxial. Birefringence and the optic axes therefore act as structural probes, as in polarizing microscopy of minerals.

name: Valley-selective circular dichroism in TMD monolayers
summary: Broken inversion in MoS2- and WSe2-type monolayers gives opposite Berry curvature and orbital moment at the K and K' valleys. With C3 symmetry this makes σ+ light excite only K and σ− only K'. Helicity therefore writes and reads valley polarization (valleytronics) and reveals the valley Zeeman splitting.

name: Magneto-optics: Faraday and Kerr rotation read M
summary: Magnetization makes the dielectric tensor gyrotropic, with an antisymmetric off-diagonal part proportional to M. The two circular polarizations then see different indices, rotating linear polarization in transmission (Faraday) and reflection (MOKE). Kerr microscopy images domains and skyrmions, and garnet ferrimagnets are used in optical isolators.

name: Nematics as field-switchable birefringent wave plates
summary: A nematic is a uniaxial birefringent medium with its optic axis along the director. Jones-calculus retardation between crossed polarizers, switched by the field-driven Fréedericksz transition, is how every LCD works. Cholesterics add selective Bragg reflection of one circular polarization, and q-plates with a patterned director imprint Pancharatnam–Berry phases.

name: Quantized conductance as electron-waveguide mode counting
summary: In the Landauer–Büttiker picture a point contact is an electron waveguide. Each transverse mode that rises above cutoff as the contact widens adds 2e²/h to the conductance, just as TE/TM modes open in a metal waveguide.
breaks: Electrons are fermions filled up to E_F, so only modes at the Fermi energy carry current and the contact resistance h/(2e²N) is intrinsic. Spin degeneracy and interactions (the 0.7 anomaly) have no counterpart in a lossless EM waveguide.
sources: van Wees et al. (1988). "Quantized conductance of point contacts in a two-dimensional electron gas". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 60, 848. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.60.848](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.60.848)
Landauer (1957). "Spatial Variation of Currents and Fields Due to Localized Scatterers in Metallic Conduction". *IBM J. Res. Dev.* 1, 223. [doi:10.1147/rd.13.0223](https://doi.org/10.1147/rd.13.0223)

name: Graphene's universal πα absorption
summary: Interband transitions of massless Dirac electrons give a frequency-independent sheet conductivity e²/4ħ. Putting it into the Fresnel transmission of a conducting sheet shows that a suspended monolayer absorbs πα≈2.3% of visible light, so a transmission measurement reads off the fine-structure constant.

name: Long Josephson junction as a superconducting stripline
summary: A long Josephson junction is a parallel-plate transmission line that carries a slow Swihart mode. Its nonlinear phase obeys the sine-Gordon equation, whose kink solitons are fluxons each carrying one flux quantum. Superconducting coplanar resonators and junction-embedded transmission lines are the microwave hardware of circuit QED and traveling-wave parametric amplifiers.
sources: Josephson (1962). "Possible new effects in superconductive tunnelling". *Phys. Lett.* 1, 251. [doi:10.1016/0031-9163(62)91369-0](https://doi.org/10.1016/0031-9163(62)91369-0)

name: Axion electrodynamics in topological insulators
summary: A 3D topological insulator adds a θE·B term to the Maxwell Lagrangian, with θ=π fixed by time reversal. This gives a quantized magnetoelectric effect, image magnetic monopoles and a half-quantized surface Hall conductance once T is broken at the surface. THz Faraday and Kerr rotations quantized in units of α are the observable signature.
map: \mathcal L_\theta=\frac{\theta e^2}{2\pi h}\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf B,\ \theta=\pi,\ \sigma_{xy}^{\rm surf}=\frac{e^2}{2h}
sources: Qi & Zhang (2011). "Topological insulators and superconductors". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 83, 1057. [arXiv:1008.2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/1008.2026)
Hasan & Kane (2010). "Colloquium: Topological insulators". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 82, 3045. [arXiv:1002.3895](https://arxiv.org/abs/1002.3895)

name: Emergent electromagnetism of skyrmions
summary: A conduction electron whose spin follows a magnetic texture picks up a Berry phase that acts as an emergent vector potential. Each skyrmion carries one emergent flux quantum h/e, which produces the topological Hall effect, and moving skyrmions induce an emergent electric field.

name: London equation: the vector potential gives the photon a mass
summary: In a superconductor the supercurrent is proportional to the vector potential, which is gauge invariant only once the condensate phase gradient is included. Combined with Ampère's law this expels B over the London depth (the Meissner effect): a frequency-independent counterpart of the skin depth, and the condensed-matter case of the Anderson–Higgs mechanism.
sources: Meissner & Ochsenfeld (1933). "Ein neuer Effekt bei Eintritt der Supraleitfähigkeit". *Naturwissenschaften* 21, 787. [doi:10.1007/BF01504252](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01504252)
Bardeen, Cooper & Schrieffer (1957). "Theory of Superconductivity". *Phys. Rev.* 108, 1175. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.108.1175](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.108.1175)

name: Gauge-invariant phase difference and flux quantization
summary: Josephson physics depends on the gauge-invariant phase difference, in which the line integral of the vector potential enters as an Aharonov–Bohm-type phase. Fluxoid quantization in units of h/2e follows, and so does the fact that SQUIDs read out the loop integral of A. The AC Josephson relation ties voltage to frequency, which is the basis of the voltage standard.
sources: Josephson (1962). "Possible new effects in superconductive tunnelling". *Phys. Lett.* 1, 251. [doi:10.1016/0031-9163(62)91369-0](https://doi.org/10.1016/0031-9163(62)91369-0)

name: Chiral anomaly driven by the invariant E·B
summary: Parallel E and B pump charge between Weyl nodes of opposite chirality at a rate set by the Lorentz invariant E·B (the dual-field invariant of covariant electrodynamics), through the chiral lowest Landau level. This is the Adler–Bell–Jackiw anomaly in a crystal (Nielsen–Ninomiya), and it predicts negative longitudinal magnetoresistance, which current-jetting artefacts complicate.
sources: Xu et al. (2015). "Discovery of a Weyl fermion semimetal and topological Fermi arcs". *Science* 349, 613. [arXiv:1502.03807](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.03807)

name: Magnetostatic energy, demagnetizing fields and domains
summary: Describing a magnetized body by its bound magnetic charges and currents gives the demagnetizing field and its dipolar self-energy. That energy produces shape anisotropy and, balanced against exchange and crystalline anisotropy, breaks ferromagnets into domains and stabilizes bubble and dipolar-skyrmion textures.
map: \mathbf H_d=-N\mathbf M,\ E_d=-\frac{\mu_0}{2}\int\mathbf M\cdot\mathbf H_d\,dV,\ \rho_m=-\nabla\cdot\mathbf M

name: Coulomb blockade from dot capacitance
summary: Adding one electron to a quantum dot costs the charging energy e²/2C. C and the dot–gate capacitance matrix come from electrostatic boundary-value problems, and gate-defined dots are designed with Poisson/Laplace solvers. Blockade needs E_C≫k_BT and tunnel resistances well above h/e², and the capacitances set the shape of the Coulomb diamonds.
map: E_C=\frac{e^2}{2C},\ C_{\rm disk}=8\epsilon r,\ k_BT\ll E_C,\ R_t\gg h/e^2
sources: Hanson et al. (2007). "Spins in few-electron quantum dots". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 79, 1217. [arXiv:cond-mat/0610433](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0610433)

name: Drude: one response function for optics and DC transport
summary: The Drude permittivity of fields-in-matter and the Drude conductivity of transport are the same causal response function. The DC resistivity, the plasma edge in reflectivity and the free-carrier absorption are three views of it. Kramers–Kronig relations and the f-sum rule let infrared spectra be read as transport.

name: Lorentz oscillator = polar optical phonon (LST relation)
summary: The Lorentz-oscillator permittivity of an ionic crystal is the response of its polar optical phonons. The macroscopic field splits LO from TO modes (Lyddane–Sachs–Teller relation), gives total reflection in the reststrahlen band between them, and mixes phonons with photons into phonon-polaritons.

name: Rytova–Keldysh screening and 2D exciton binding
summary: Thin-film electrostatics of a polarizable sheet gives a potential that is logarithmic below the screening length r0 and 1/r beyond it. This explains the non-hydrogenic Rydberg series and the ~0.5 eV exciton binding energies of monolayer TMDs. Changing the dielectric surroundings (encapsulation) shifts the gap and the binding energy, an approach called Coulomb engineering.

name: Quantum origin of dia-, para- and ferromagnetic χ
summary: The susceptibility that fields-in-matter takes as an input is quantum mechanical. By the Bohr–van Leeuwen theorem, classical statistics gives zero magnetization. Condensed matter supplies the actual sources: Landau diamagnetism, Pauli and Curie paramagnetism, and exchange-driven order. For free electrons the Landau term is −1/3 of the Pauli term.
map: \mathbf M=\chi_m\mathbf H,\ \chi_{\rm P}=\mu_0\mu_B^2g(E_F),\ \chi_{\rm L}=-\tfrac13\chi_{\rm P},\ \chi_{\rm C}=\frac{C}{T}

name: Weiss molecular field as mean-field exchange
summary: The fields-in-matter note treats ferromagnetism phenomenologically, through a huge χ and hysteretic M(H). Exchange theory supplies the cause: Weiss's molecular field is the mean field of Heisenberg exchange, which gives a Curie–Weiss susceptibility above T_c and spontaneous magnetization below it.
map: H=-J\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\mathbf S_i\cdot\mathbf S_j\ \to\ \mathbf B_{\rm W}=\lambda\mathbf M,\ \chi=\frac{C}{T-\theta_{CW}}

name: Optical gap 2Δ and the Ferrell–Glover–Tinkham sum rule
summary: A superconductor absorbs only above ħω=2Δ (Mattis–Bardeen), and far-infrared measurements of this edge were among the first gap measurements. The spectral weight that disappears from σ1 collapses into a superfluid δ(ω) whose weight fixes the London penetration depth. This links fields-in-matter response theory to the London depth and BCS.
sources: Bardeen, Cooper & Schrieffer (1957). "Theory of Superconductivity". *Phys. Rev.* 108, 1175. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.108.1175](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.108.1175)

name: Modern theory of polarization: P as a Berry phase
summary: For a periodic crystal the bulk polarization P is not well defined as a sum of dipoles. It is well defined, up to the polarization quantum eR/Ω, as the Berry phase of the occupied Bloch states (King-Smith–Vanderbilt). Changes in P (piezoelectric, ferroelectric, Thouless pumping) are what DFT computes and what experiments measure.
map: \mathbf P=-\frac{e}{(2\pi)^3}\sum_n\int_{\rm BZ}i\langle u_{n\mathbf k}|\nabla_{\mathbf k}u_{n\mathbf k}\rangle\,d^3k\ (\mathrm{mod}\ e\mathbf R/\Omega)

name: Diode lasers: inversion between quasi-Fermi levels
summary: In a semiconductor laser, population inversion is a separation of the electron and hole quasi-Fermi levels in a forward-biased p–n junction. Gain appears when the Bernard–Duraffourg condition holds. Double heterostructures and quantum wells confine both carriers and light, and Fermi–Dirac band filling takes the place of two-level atoms.

name: Exciton-polariton lasing without inversion
summary: When excitons couple strongly to microcavity photons they form polaritons, which can condense and emit coherent light with no population inversion: a polariton laser. The large exciton binding energy of TMD monolayers allows room-temperature polaritons, and polariton condensation in TMDs is under active study.

name: Laser threshold as a Ginzburg–Landau transition
summary: Near threshold the single-mode laser amplitude obeys a Ginzburg–Landau equation: the field is the order parameter and gain minus loss plays the role of reduced temperature (Haken; DeGiorgio–Scully). Above threshold a U(1) phase is chosen spontaneously, and diffusion of that phase, a Goldstone-like mode, sets the Schawlow–Townes linewidth.
breaks: A laser is driven-dissipative and far from equilibrium, and its noise comes from spontaneous emission, not temperature. With few modes there is no true symmetry breaking, so the phase diffuses and the linewidth is finite. There is no gauge field, hence no Meissner or Higgs counterpart.
sources: Schawlow & Townes (1958). "Infrared and Optical Masers". *Phys. Rev.* 112, 1940. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.112.1940](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.112.1940)

name: Photonic crystals: Bloch band theory for light
summary: Yablonovitch and John applied Bloch's theorem to Maxwell's equations in periodic dielectrics. The result is photonic band structures, band gaps, defect states and slow-light band edges, computed with the electronic-structure toolkit (plane-wave expansion, tight-binding coupled resonators).
map: \nabla\times\frac{1}{\epsilon(\mathbf r)}\nabla\times\mathbf H=\frac{\omega^2}{c^2}\mathbf H,\ \mathbf H_{\mathbf k}=e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r}\mathbf u_{\mathbf k}(\mathbf r)
breaks: The field is a transverse vector field with no interactions and no Pauli exclusion. The eigenvalue is ω² rather than E, and Maxwell scale invariance lets the gap scale with the lattice constant. Full 3D gaps need a high index contrast.
sources: Yablonovitch (1987). "Inhibited Spontaneous Emission in Solid-State Physics and Electronics". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 58, 2059. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.58.2059](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.58.2059)
Bloch (1929). "Über die Quantenmechanik der Elektronen in Kristallgittern". *Z. Phys.* 52, 555. [doi:10.1007/BF01339455](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01339455)

name: Graphene plasmons and hBN hyperbolic polaritons
summary: Graphene is a gate-tunable 2D plasmonic medium with a √q dispersion set by E_F. Near-field microscopy images its plasmons at wavelengths far below the free-space wavelength. Inside its reststrahlen bands hBN is a natural hyperbolic medium (ε_∥ε_⊥<0), so van der Waals heterostructures act as natural metamaterials.

name: Quantum-dot emission controlled by the local density of states
summary: A quantum dot's spontaneous-emission rate follows the local optical density of states. Photonic band gaps suppress it, and photonic-crystal nanocavities and plasmonic nanoantennas raise it (the Purcell effect). This underlies deterministic single-photon sources and vacuum Rabi splitting with single dots.
sources: Yablonovitch (1987). "Inhibited Spontaneous Emission in Solid-State Physics and Electronics". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 58, 2059. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.58.2059](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.58.2059)

name: χ(2) selection rules and SHG as a symmetry probe
summary: χ(2) is a polar third-rank tensor. It vanishes in the 11 centrosymmetric point groups and in 432, leaving the same 20 classes that allow piezoelectricity. SHG therefore detects broken inversion (ferroelectric and other polar orders, surfaces, odd versus even layer number in 2D crystals), and quasi-phase-matching relies on periodically poled ferroelectric domains.
sources: Franken et al. (1961). "Generation of Optical Harmonics". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 7, 118. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.7.118](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.7.118)

name: Haldane–Raghu: quantum Hall physics carried into light
summary: Haldane and Raghu (2008) carried the Chern-band physics of the quantum Hall effect and Haldane's 1988 lattice model into gyromagnetic photonic crystals. One-way microwave edge states were then seen in YIG (Wang et al. 2009), which founded topological photonics. The field later imported quantum spin Hall, valley Hall, Floquet and higher-order phases.
sources: Haldane (1988). "Model for a Quantum Hall Effect without Landau Levels: Condensed-Matter Realization of the 'Parity Anomaly'". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 61, 2015. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.61.2015](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.61.2015)
Ozawa et al. (2019). "Topological photonics". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 91, 015006. [arXiv:1802.04173](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.04173)

name: Berry curvature and Chern numbers of Maxwell Bloch modes
summary: The Bloch eigenmodes of the periodic Maxwell operator have a Berry connection and curvature, defined with the ε- or μ-weighted inner product, and their Chern numbers are integers exactly as for electron bands (TKNN). Magneto-optic gyrotropy breaks time reversal in place of a magnetic field, and bulk–edge correspondence fixes the number of one-way edge modes.
map: C=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\rm BZ}\Omega(\mathbf k)\,d^2k\in\mathbb Z,\ \Omega=\nabla_{\mathbf k}\times i\langle u_{\mathbf k}|\nabla_{\mathbf k}u_{\mathbf k}\rangle,\ N_{\rm edge}=\Delta C
sources: Thouless, Kohmoto, Nightingale & den Nijs (1982). "Quantized Hall Conductance in a Two-Dimensional Periodic Potential". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 49, 405. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.49.405](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.49.405)
Ozawa et al. (2019). "Topological photonics". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 91, 015006. [arXiv:1802.04173](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.04173)

name: Photonic quantum spin Hall and valley Hall insulators
summary: Photonic crystals and coupled-resonator lattices copy the quantum spin Hall effect with a pseudospin. That pseudospin comes from TE/TM degeneracy (ε=μ), C6 crystalline symmetry or the circulation direction in a ring. The result is helical edge states that pass around sharp corners, much like the edges of a Z2 topological insulator.
map: H_{\rm KM}\leftrightarrow H_{\rm photonic}(\sigma_{\rm pseudo}),\ \nu\in\mathbb Z_2\leftrightarrow C_\uparrow=-C_\downarrow
breaks: Photons are bosons with T^2=+1, so there is no Kramers degeneracy. The protection lasts only while the engineered pseudospin symmetry does, and lattice-scale disorder can couple the edge modes. With no Fermi level, the edge states must be excited at a chosen frequency.
sources: Kane & Mele (2005). "Z2 Topological Order and the Quantum Spin Hall Effect". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 95, 146802. [arXiv:cond-mat/0506581](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0506581)
Ozawa et al. (2019). "Topological photonics". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 91, 015006. [arXiv:1802.04173](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.04173)

name: High-harmonic generation in solids probes band structure
summary: Strong-field HHG, first developed in atomic gases, also works in bulk crystals (ZnO and others). There it comes from intraband currents of Bloch-oscillating carriers in nonparabolic bands plus interband recombination, the three-step model adapted to bands. The cutoff grows linearly with field rather than quadratically, and harmonic spectra allow all-optical reconstruction of the band structure.
sources: Krausz & Ivanov (2009). "Attosecond physics". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 81, 163. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.81.163](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.81.163)

name: Ultrafast demagnetization and spintronic THz emitters
summary: Femtosecond pulses demagnetize Ni in under a picosecond (Beaurepaire et al. 1996) and switch ferrimagnets such as GdFeCo all-optically. The ultrafast spin currents involved are converted to charge currents by the inverse spin Hall effect, which makes ferromagnet/heavy-metal bilayers broadband THz emitters. Whether spin-flip scattering or superdiffusive transport dominates is still debated.

name: Light-induced transient superconductivity (contested)
summary: Mid-infrared pumping of apical-oxygen phonons in stripe-ordered LESCO and in YBCO produces a transient c-axis optical response resembling superconductivity above T_c, with similar claims for K3C60. The interpretation is contested: heating, inhomogeneity and the analysis of reflectivity are all debated. Reports of transient Meissner-like diamagnetism are recent and unconfirmed.

name: Floquet engineering of Chern bands with circular light
summary: A strong circularly polarized drive dresses Bloch bands. In the high-frequency expansion it opens a Haldane-type mass at Dirac points and creates Chern bands (Oka–Aoki). Floquet–Bloch states have been seen on topological-insulator surfaces by tr-ARPES, and a light-induced anomalous Hall effect in graphene. Helical-waveguide photonic Floquet insulators use the same idea.
sources: Haldane (1988). "Model for a Quantum Hall Effect without Landau Levels: Condensed-Matter Realization of the 'Parity Anomaly'". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 61, 2015. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.61.2015](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.61.2015)

name: X-ray diffraction as coherent Thomson scattering
summary: X-ray crystallography is Thomson scattering from the electron density, summed coherently over the lattice. The atomic form factor is the Fourier transform of an atom's charge density, Bragg/Laue conditions select the reciprocal-lattice vectors, and the intensity goes as the squared structure factor.
map: I(\mathbf q)\propto\frac{d\sigma_T}{d\Omega}|F(\mathbf q)|^2,\ F(\mathbf G)=\sum_jf_je^{i\mathbf G\cdot\mathbf r_j},\ 2d\sin\theta=n\lambda

name: Raman and Brillouin scattering as phonon spectroscopy
summary: Inelastic light scattering, with energy and momentum conserved, measures optical phonons near q=0 (Raman, with selection rules set by the point group) and acoustic phonons (Brillouin, whose shift gives the sound velocity). The Stokes/anti-Stokes ratio gives the temperature through the Bose factor. Electrostrictive coupling to the same phonons drives stimulated Brillouin scattering in fibres.

name: VLBI and EHT as van Cittert–Zernike imaging
summary: Radio interferometry measures visibilities that are Fourier components of source brightness, per van Cittert–Zernike; the EHT imaged the M87 and Sgr A* shadows from sparse coverage.

name: Interferometry and direct imaging of exoplanets
summary: Van Cittert–Zernike coherence underlies interferometric imaging and nulling, while coronagraphs use diffraction control and apodization to suppress starlight for direct imaging.

name: Hanbury Brown–Twiss stellar intensity interferometry
summary: Intensity correlations measured by Hanbury Brown and Twiss gave stellar angular diameters, founding photon-statistics optics and being revived with Cherenkov telescope arrays.

name: Diffraction limit and adaptive optics at the Galactic Centre
summary: Telescope resolution is set by the diffraction limit, and adaptive optics corrects atmospheric phase errors to track stellar orbits around Sgr A*.

name: Lensing as geometric optics in curved spacetime
summary: Light follows null geodesics, equivalent to rays in a medium with effective refractive index n = 1 − 2Φ/c²; the lens equation and Fermat's principle mirror thin-lens optics.
breaks: Lenses have no focal point (the deflection is not linear in impact parameter), and the lens is an extended mass whose profile fixes the images; strong-field lensing leaves the geometric-optics limit.

name: Telescope optics and survey instruments
summary: Aberration theory and wide-field optical design set the imaging performance of survey telescopes like ZTF and Rubin used for transient discovery.

name: Wave optics of lensing and fringes
summary: Lensing of coherent waves (FRBs, gravitational waves) shows interference between images, and diffraction from point lenses gives fringes when wavelength approaches the Schwarzschild radius, as in Fresnel optics.
breaks: Geometric optics is recovered only for w much greater than 1; strong dependence on lens profile and no analogue of aberration-free focusing.

name: Stokes parameters and E/B polarization
summary: CMB polarization is described with Stokes Q and U, decomposed into curl-free E and divergence-free B modes, a spin-2 field analogous to optical polarization states.

name: Faraday rotation and polarimetry of jets
summary: Birefringence of magnetized plasma rotates linear polarization as λ², letting radio polarimetry measure magnetic fields in jets, the Galaxy and intergalactic gas.

name: FRB dispersion and Faraday rotation as plasma probes
summary: Plasma refractive index gives frequency-dependent delay (dispersion measure) and Faraday rotation, which together weigh intergalactic baryons and magnetic fields along FRB sightlines.

name: Wave propagation in cold plasma
summary: The cold-plasma dispersion relation of EM waves, with cutoff at the plasma frequency, gives FRB pulse delay and scattering broadening by turbulent plasma.

name: Solar magnetic fields and MHD
summary: Maxwell's equations with induction and Ampère's law in the low-frequency limit give magnetohydrodynamics for solar fields, flux freezing and reconnection driving flares.
breaks: Displacement current is dropped and ideal conductivity assumed; reconnection requires non-ideal terms.

name: Relativistic beaming and Doppler boosting
summary: Lorentz transformations of fields and radiation give aberration and Doppler boosting of jet emission, explaining superluminal motion and blazar brightness.

name: Laser frequency combs for radial velocity
summary: Laser frequency combs and microresonator Kerr combs give precise wavelength calibration for spectrographs, targeting cm/s radial-velocity precision needed for Earth-like planets.

name: Astrophysical masers and lasers
summary: Population inversion and stimulated emission occur naturally as masers in star-forming regions and evolved-star envelopes, with narrow bright lines used for distances and kinematics.
breaks: Masers lack an optical cavity and are single-pass amplifiers, with no mode selection or coherence like a laser.

name: Radiation processes power high-energy sources
summary: Synchrotron, bremsstrahlung and inverse-Compton emission from relativistic charges, derived from Liénard–Wiechert fields, underlie GRBs, AGN jets, cosmic-ray signatures and FRBs.

name: Air-Cherenkov detection of cosmic rays
summary: Cherenkov light from air showers triggered by cosmic rays and gamma rays is imaged by IACTs such as H.E.S.S. and CTA, reconstructing primary energy and direction.

name: Cherenkov light detects neutrinos
summary: IceCube and KM3NeT detect Cherenkov light from relativistic charged secondaries of neutrino interactions in ice and water, using the cos θ = 1/(nβ) cone to reconstruct direction.

name: Neutrino telescopes rely on the Cherenkov effect
summary: The Frank–Tamm photon yield and the refractive-index dispersion of ice and seawater set the light output and detector response of neutrino telescopes.

name: Pulsar spin-down as magnetic dipole radiation
summary: A rotating magnetic dipole radiates at the rotation frequency, giving the braking index n=3 and characteristic age estimates for pulsars.

name: Synchrotron emission from AGN jets
summary: Relativistic electrons spiraling in jet magnetic fields emit beamed synchrotron radiation, giving power-law spectra, high polarization and Doppler boosting in blazars.

name: Synchrotron afterglow and fireball emission
summary: GRB afterglows are synchrotron emission from shock-accelerated electrons in a decelerating relativistic blast wave, with broken power-law spectra whose breaks map to electron energy and magnetic field.

name: Pulsar and magnetar radiation
summary: Pulsar magnetic-dipole braking uses the dipole radiation formula, and coherent curvature and synchrotron emission from magnetospheric particles produce radio and gamma-ray pulses.

name: Synchrotron in supernova remnants
summary: Radio and X-ray synchrotron emission from electrons accelerated at remnant shocks reveals magnetic field amplification and particle acceleration, linking to cosmic-ray origin.

name: Photon–baryon tight coupling via Thomson
summary: Thomson scattering couples photons to baryons before recombination, producing the acoustic oscillations; the visibility function and Silk damping follow from the scattering mean free path.

name: Thomson scattering polarizes the CMB
summary: Thomson scattering of anisotropic radiation by free electrons, with its dipole angular dependence, generates CMB linear polarization (E modes) at recombination and reionization.

name: Eddington limit and Compton coronae in AGN
summary: Thomson-limited radiation pressure caps accretion luminosity, and Comptonization of disk photons in hot coronae produces AGN X-ray power-law spectra.

name: Sunyaev–Zel'dovich inverse-Compton scattering
summary: CMB photons Compton-scattered by hot intracluster electrons gain energy, distorting the blackbody spectrum; the Kompaneets treatment of Compton scattering yields the thermal SZ signal used to find clusters.

name: Inverse Compton and synchrotron cooling of cosmic rays
summary: Relativistic electrons lose energy by synchrotron and inverse-Compton scattering on CMB and starlight, steepening spectra and producing TeV gamma rays, which limits the lifetime of cosmic-ray electrons.

name: Compton scattering in relativistic outflows
summary: Inverse-Compton and Thomson scattering set photospheric opacity and high-energy afterglow components in GRB fireballs; the Thomson optical depth fixes the compactness constraint on Lorentz factors.

name: Rayleigh and Mie scattering in exoplanet hazes
summary: Rayleigh slopes and Mie scattering by clouds and hazes shape transmission spectra, muting molecular features and giving blue-slope signatures, as for Earth's blue sky.

name: Electron-scattering opacity and Eddington limit
summary: Thomson scattering opacity sets radiation pressure in stellar interiors and the Eddington luminosity limiting massive stars and accretion.

name: Partial coherence suppresses instabilities
summary: Random phase plates and induced spatial incoherence reduce speckle-driven filamentation and parametric instabilities in laser plasmas by controlling coherence.

name: Interferometry for plasma density
summary: Interferometers measure line-integrated density through the plasma refractive index. Mach–Zehnder and two-colour interferometry are standard on tokamaks and laser plasmas.
